p1.key: Both routes go from the same reactants to the same final products, so ΔH1 = ΔH + ΔH2, where ΔH2 takes the decomposition products on to the final state. Hence ΔH = ΔH1 − ΔH2.
Target = ½[(second) − (first)]: ΔH = ½(66.4 − 180.4) = ½(−114) = −57 kJ.
Ionization (I) and atomization (II) need energy. The first electron affinity of Cl (III) and forming the lattice from gaseous ions (IV) release energy: III and IV.
C(s) + ½O2(g) → CO(g) = (first) − ½(second): ΔHf = −393 − ½(−588) = −393 + 294 = −99 kJ mol−1.
ΔH is negative, so more energy is released forming the product's bonds than is absorbed breaking the reactants' bonds: bonds broken < bonds formed.
Bonds broken: 2 H—Cl = 862 kJ. Bonds formed: H—H + Cl—Cl = 436 + 242 = 678 kJ. ΔH = 862 − 678 = +184 kJ.

Lattice enthalpy rises with ionic charge and falls with ionic size. The 1+ salts are lowest (CsF < LiF, because Cs<sup>+</sup> is larger). The 2+ salts are higher, with CaCl<sub>2</sub> < CaF<sub>2</sub> because Cl<sup>−</sup> is larger than F<sup>−</sup>.
Broken: C=C + H–H = 612 + 436 = 1048. Formed: C–C + 2 C–H = 348 + 824 = 1172 (the other four C–H bonds are unchanged). ΔH = 1048 − 1172 = −124 kJ mol−1.
ΔH = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed) = (N≡N + 3 H–H) − (6 N–H) = x + 3y − 6z. Two NH3 molecules contain six N–H bonds.
Adding all four equations gives H2(g) + S(s) + 2O2(g) → H2SO4(l) (SO2, SO3 and H2O cancel). ΔHf = −298 − 98 − 130 − 286 = −812 kJ.
Break one O–O (146); form ½ O=O (½ × 496 = 248). The O–H bonds are unchanged. ΔH = 146 − 248 = −102 kJ.

p1.key: Ca2+ has double the charge of Li+, giving stronger attraction and a larger lattice enthalpy. Statement I would make LiF’s value larger, so it does not explain it.

p1.key: 2CuO → 2Cu + O2: +2(156) = +312; 2Cu + ½O2 → Cu2O: −170. Net: 2CuO → Cu2O + ½O2, ΔH = 312 − 170 = +142 kJ.
Reverse MgO formation (+602) and add H2O formation (−242): ΔH = +602 − 242 = +360 kJ.

Bond enthalpy refers to breaking one mole of bonds with everything gaseous: CH<sub>4</sub>(g) → CH<sub>3</sub>(g) + H(g) breaks exactly one C–H bond. The others involve several bonds and/or solid carbon.
Standard enthalpy of formation: 1 mol of a compound formed from its elements in their standard states.
C + O2 → CO2 (−x), then reverse CO + ½O2 → CO2 (+y): ΔH = −x + y = y − x.
Bonds broken: 2 H–H + 1 O=O = 2x + y. Bonds formed: 2 H2O contain 4 O–H = 4z. ΔH = broken − formed = 2x + y − 4z.
Target = 2 × (S + O2 → SO2) + (2SO2 + O2 → 2SO3): ΔH = 2(−300) + (−200) = −800 kJ.
ΔH = ΔHf(P4O10) − ΔHf(P4O6) = −3000 − (−1600) = −1400 kJ mol−1 (O2 is an element, ΔHf = 0).
Hess's law: S → SO3 (−395), then reverse SO2 → SO3 (+98). ΔH = −395 + 98 = −297 kJ mol⁻¹.

ΔH<sub>c</sub> = ΣΔH<sub>f</sub>(products) − ΣΔH<sub>f</sub>(reactants) = 6(−394) + 3(−286) − (+49) = −3271 kJ mol⁻¹ (ΔH<sub>f</sub>(O<sub>2</sub>) = 0). A doubles everything (2 mol benzene); D has the signs reversed.

Lattice enthalpy links 1 mol of ionic solid with its separated gaseous ions: Mg²⁺(g) + O²⁻(g) and MgO(s). A is ΔH<sub>f</sub>; B gives a gaseous product. (The current IB convention defines it as the endothermic reverse, MgO(s) → Mg²⁺(g) + O²⁻(g).)
p1.flag: Old definition (exothermic lattice formation); 2025 IB defines lattice enthalpy as lattice dissociation.

p1.key: Reverse 2 × formation of NO2 (2 × +57 = +114), then form N2O4 (+9). ΔH = ΔHf(N2O4) − 2ΔHf(NO2) = +9 − 2(−57) = +123 kJ. A uses +57 by mistake.
Target = eqn 2 − 2 × eqn 1: reverse 2S + 2O2 → 2SO2 (+600) and add 2S + 3O2 → 2SO3 (−800). ΔH = −800 + 600 = −200 kJ.
ΔH<sub>f</sub>° forms 1 mol of compound from its elements in their standard states: Ca(s) + F<sub>2</sub>(g) → CaF<sub>2</sub>(s). A uses gaseous Ca and product; C and D start from ions.
Adding the two equations gives H2 + O2 → H2O2, ΔH = x + y. Decomposition is the reverse: ΔH = −x − y.
Breaking a bond requires energy to overcome the attraction (endothermic). Forming a bond releases the same amount of energy (exothermic).

A bond enthalpy is for breaking one mole of a particular bond with everything in the gaseous state. D breaks exactly one C–H bond: CH4(g) → CH3(g) + H(g). C breaks four (≈ 4 × 412); A and B involve solid carbon or are not balanced as single-bond breaking. D.
Balanced: 3Mg + KClO3 → 3MgO + KCl. ΔH = ΣΔHf(products) − ΣΔHf(reactants) = [3(−602) + (−437)] − (−391) = −2243 + 391 = −1852 kJ (ΔHf(Mg) = 0).

ΔHf⦵ forms exactly 1 mol of compound from its elements in their standard states. C does this for butan-1-ol: 4C(s) + 5H2(g) + ½O2(g) → C4H9OH(l). A and B start from compounds; D forms 2 mol (2ΔHf). C.

Lattice enthalpy (IB definition) is the enthalpy change to separate 1 mol of solid ionic compound into its gaseous ions: NaCl(s) → Na+(g) + Cl−(g). A. B is the reverse of formation; C starts from gaseous NaCl.
Hess's law: C → CO2 (−394), then reverse CO → CO2 (+283). ΔH = −394 + 283 = −111 kJ.
The target needs 2 CH4 → 2 HCHO (2x), then 2 HCHO → 2 HCOOH (2y), then 2 HCOOH → (COOH)2 once (z). Check O2: 2 + 1 + ½ = 3½. ΔH = 2x + 2y + z.
The equation burns 2 mol H2, so per mole of H2 burned (= per mole of H2O(l) formed) ΔH = −572/2 = −286 kJ mol−1. Combustion is exothermic, so A. C and D are wrong because −572 kJ refers to 2 mol H2O.

Lattice enthalpy relates 1 mol of ionic solid to its separated gaseous ions. This paper uses the formation direction; the current IB data booklet quotes the endothermic dissociation direction. A is ionization energy, B is enthalpy of formation, C is melting. D.
p1.flag: old definition (formation from gaseous ions); 2025 guide uses dissociation

p1.key: Target = equation 2 − 2 × equation 1. Reversing 2 × eq 1 gives 4FeO → 4Fe + 2O2; adding eq 2 cancels the 4Fe: ΔH = −1648 − 2(−544) = −560 kJ.
Breaking bonds always requires energy (endothermic); forming bonds always releases energy (exothermic).
Lattice enthalpy converts one mole of an ionic solid into its separate gaseous ions: AgI(s) → Ag⁺(g) + I⁻(g). Aqueous ions (C) describe dissolving instead.
Bond enthalpy is the energy to break one mole of a bond in a gaseous molecule into gaseous atoms: HBr(g) → H(g) + Br(g). Forming Br<sub>2</sub> or liquid bromine involves extra changes.
ΔHf(C2H6) = 2ΔHc(C) + 3ΔHc(H2) − ΔHc(C2H6) = [(−2x) + (−3y)] − (−z). Don't forget the coefficients 2 and 3 (A ignores them).
Lattice enthalpy links gaseous ions with the solid lattice (shown here in the formation direction, X⁺(g) + Y⁻(g) → XY(s)). Electron affinity is Y(g) + e⁻ → Y⁻(g). B is the only row with both correct.
I: Na(g) → Na⁺(g) + e⁻, the ionization energy (up). II: Cl(g) + e⁻ → Cl⁻(g), the electron affinity (down, exothermic). III links the gaseous ions to NaCl(s): the lattice enthalpy.
ΔHf(CH4) = ΔHc(C) + 2ΔHc(H2) − ΔHc(CH4) = −390 + 2(−286) − (−890) = −72 kJ.
Electron affinity is the enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous atoms each gain an electron to form gaseous 1− ions. The gaseous state is essential to the definition. A describes electronegativity.
ΔH = ΔHf(C2H6) − ΔHf(C2H4) = −85 − (+52) = −137 kJ mol−1.

The standard enthalpy of combustion is for exactly 1 mol of fuel burned completely, with products in their standard states. At 298 K water is a liquid, so H<sub>2</sub>O(l) is required. C uses 2 mol of fuel, and A and D give gaseous water.
Target = equation 2 − ½ × equation 1. Equation 1 is reversed and halved, so it contributes −0.5x: ΔH = y − 0.5x.

Combine ½(equation a) + (equation b) − ½(equation c). This burns HCOOH and C2H5OH, then reverses the combustion of 1 mol of ester. CO2 and O2 cancel and one H2O is left as a product, so ΔH = ½a + b − ½c.

Lattice enthalpy (IB convention, endothermic) is the enthalpy change when 1 mol of a solid ionic compound is separated into its gaseous ions, for example NaCl(s) → Na+(g) + Cl−(g). D describes the enthalpy of formation.
Reverse the Fe2O3 formation equation (−x) and add three times the CO combustion equation (3y). The 1½O2 cancels, giving Fe2O3 + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO2, so ΔH = 3y − x.
ΔH = bonds broken − bonds formed = (436 + 243) − 2(432) = 679 − 864 = −185 kJ mol−1. Two H–Cl bonds are formed.

Step X goes from Mg(g) to Mg2+(g) + 2e−, which is the sum of the 1st and 2nd ionization energies. Step Y links MgO(s) and the gaseous ions (lattice enthalpy). Step Z goes from the elements in their standard states to MgO(s) (enthalpy of formation).

Formation must start from the elements in their standard states, C(s, graphite), H<sub>2</sub>(g) and O<sub>2</sub>(g), and make 1 mol of product: C(s) + 2H<sub>2</sub>(g) + ½O<sub>2</sub>(g) → CH<sub>3</sub>OH(l). Gaseous C atoms or H atoms are not standard states.
Target = ½(Al equation) − ½(Fe equation): form 1 mol Al2O3 and reverse the formation of 1 mol Fe2O3. ΔH = ½(−3338) − ½(−1644) = −1669 + 822 = −847 kJ.
Bond enthalpies apply only to substances in the gaseous state. Reactions I and III involve only gases. Reaction II contains liquid ethanol, so its enthalpy of vaporization would also be needed.

ΔH<sub>f</sub>° forms 1 mol of compound in its standard state (CCl<sub>4</sub> is a liquid at 298 K) from its elements in their standard states, C(s, graphite) and Cl<sub>2</sub>(g): C(s) + 2Cl<sub>2</sub>(g) → CCl<sub>4</sub>(l).

ΔHf° is the enthalpy change when 1 mol of a compound in its standard state is formed from its elements in their standard states, e.g. C(s, graphite) and H2(g). A and C start from gaseous atoms; B leaves out the standard-state condition for the elements.

First electron affinity: 1 mol of gaseous atoms each gain one electron to form gaseous 1− ions, X(g) + e− → X−(g), as in C(g) + e− → C−(g). C starts from Cl2 molecules, not atoms; B is a reduction in solution; D is ionization.
Hess's law with combustion data: ΔH = Σ ΔHc(reactants) − Σ ΔHc(products). The H2 and C2H2 equations are written for 2 mol, so each is halved: 2(−394) + ½(−572) − ½(−2602) = +227 kJ.

Average bond enthalpy: break all bonds of the gaseous molecule into gaseous atoms, then divide by the number of bonds. ¼SiH<sub>4</sub>(g) → ¼Si(g) + H(g) is one Si–H bond's worth. A breaks only the first bond (a specific value); C forms H<sub>2</sub>, not atoms; D is four times the value.
Enthalpy of hydration is the enthalpy change when 1 mol of gaseous ions becomes surrounded by water: K+(g) → K+(aq). B is the enthalpy of solution, and A is the auto-ionization of water.
ΔH = 2ΔHf(H2O) − ΔHf(N2H4), because N2 and O2 are elements with ΔHf = 0. So −623 = 2(−286) − ΔHf(N2H4), giving ΔHf(N2H4) = −572 + 623 = +51 kJ.

Hydration enthalpy is for gaseous ions becoming surrounded by water: Cl−(g) → Cl−(aq). The other options start from atoms or molecules, so they include extra steps such as bond breaking or electron affinity.
Both routes go from CaCO3 to CaCl2 + H2O + CO2. Direct route then acid: ΔH + ΔH2; acid route: ΔH1. By Hess's law, ΔH + ΔH2 = ΔH1, so ΔH = ΔH1 − ΔH2.
Enthalpy of hydration is the enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous ions becomes hydrated: Na+(g) → Na+(aq). C is the (endothermic) lattice enthalpy and D is the enthalpy of solution.
Lattice enthalpy (K2O(s) → 2K+(g) + O2−(g)) = reverse of formation + atomization + ionization + electron affinities: −(−361) + 428 + 838 + 612 = +2239 kJ mol−1.
Hydration is most exothermic for the ion with the highest charge density. All four ions carry a single charge, and Li+ is the smallest, so it attracts water molecules most strongly.
ΔH = [ΔHf(IF5) + 2ΔHf(IF)] − [ΔHf(IF7) + 0]. So −89 = −840 + 2x + 941, giving 2x = −190 and x = −95 kJ mol−1. I2(s) is an element, so its ΔHf = 0.
Lattice enthalpy is the enthalpy needed to separate one mole of the solid ionic compound into its gaseous ions: MgS(s) → Mg2+(g) + S2−(g). The ions are 2+ and 2−, not 1+ and 1−.

Enthalpy of combustion is per mole of butane: C4H10 + 6½O2 → 4CO2 + 5H2O = 4 × (C combustion) + 5 × (H2 combustion) − (formation of butane), so ΔHc = 4x + 5y − z. C is for 2 mol of butane, as in the equation shown.
ΔHsol = lattice enthalpy (endothermic, solid → gaseous ions) + hydration enthalpies of all ions. MgF2 gives two F− ions: ΔHsol = 2926 − 1963 + 2(−504) = −45 kJ mol−1.

Lattice enthalpy is SrCl2(s) → Sr2+(g) + 2Cl−(g). Going round the cycle: reverse the formation step, −(−829), then +164 + 243 + 550 + 1064, then the electron-affinity step for 2Cl → 2Cl−, −698. Total = −(−829) + 164 + 243 + 550 + 1064 − 698 = +2152 kJ mol−1.
Target = equation 1 − 2 × equation 2 (reverse equation 2 and double it so the 2FeO cancel): ΔH = (−3) − 2(+11) = −25 kJ.
The first electron affinity of chlorine releases energy (Cl(g) + e− → Cl−(g) is exothermic). Atomization, ionization and lattice dissociation (A–C) all need energy, so they are endothermic.
Target = combustion of C2H4 (x) + combustion of H2 (z) − combustion of C2H6 (reverse y). The CO2 and H2O cancel, so ΔH = x − y + z.
The enthalpy of atomization is per mole of gaseous atoms formed from the element in its standard state: ½Br2(l) → Br(g). B forms 2 mol of atoms, and C and D do not give gaseous atoms.
ΔH = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed). Broken: 2CH4 has 8 C–H, plus 3 O=O. Formed: 2 C≡O, and 4H2O have 8 O–H. So ΔH = [8(414) + 3(498)] − [2(1077) + 8(463)].

Lattice enthalpy (IB convention) is the endothermic change when one mole of solid ionic compound is separated into its gaseous ions: NaCl(s) → Na+(g) + Cl−(g). C is dissolving, and A starts from a gas.
ΔH = Σ ΔHc(reactants) − Σ ΔHc(products) = −4163 − (−1411 − 2878) = +1411 + 2878 − 4163 = +126 kJ mol−1.
Hydration enthalpy becomes more exothermic with higher ionic charge and smaller radius (higher charge density): K+ < Na+ < Ca2+ < Mg2+.
Hydration enthalpy is the enthalpy change when one mole of gaseous ions dissolves in water: Na+(g) → Na+(aq).
Bond enthalpy is the energy to break one mole of bonds in gaseous molecules into gaseous atoms: HBr(g) → H(g) + Br(g). C and D re-form the elements (reverse ΔHf), not atoms.
